whyItExists.problem: Web pages need to respond to user actions — clicks, key presses, form submissions, mouse movement. Without a way to listen for and respond to these actions, pages would be entirely static.
whyItExists.solution: The browser fires events when things happen. JavaScript uses addEventListener to attach a function (handler) to an event on an element. When the event fires, the handler runs.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Responding to any user interaction: clicks, keyboard input, form submission, hover, focus, scroll, resize.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid inline event attributes (onclick='...') in HTML — they mix concerns and are harder to maintain. Prefer addEventListener in a script file.

explainModes.beginner: Events are things that happen — a button is clicked, a key is pressed, a form is submitted. addEventListener listens for an event on an element and runs a function when it happens.
explainModes.simple: element.addEventListener('click', handler) attaches a listener. The handler receives an event object with information about what happened — event.target is the element that was clicked, event.key is the key pressed.
explainModes.standard: Events bubble up the DOM — a click on a child also fires on the parent. Event delegation uses this to attach one listener to a parent that handles events from many children. event.preventDefault() stops the browser's default action. event.stopPropagation() stops bubbling.
explainModes.technical: Every element is an EventTarget. addEventListener has a third argument: {capture: true} to run in the capture phase (top-down) instead of bubble phase (bottom-up). {once: true} removes the listener after first fire. {passive: true} tells the browser the handler won't call preventDefault, enabling scroll optimisations. removeEventListener requires the exact same function reference.
explainModes.deepDive: The event loop processes events from the callback queue after the call stack is empty. Long-running synchronous code blocks events — this freezes the UI. Debouncing (delay + cancel) and throttling (max frequency) limit how often expensive handlers fire on scroll/resize/input. Custom events use new CustomEvent('name', {detail: data}) and dispatchEvent.

content.text: Instead of attaching a listener to every list item (expensive and breaks on dynamically added items), attach ONE listener to the parent and check which child was clicked.

questions.question: What is event.preventDefault() used for?
options: Stop the event from firing again
Stop the event bubbling to parent elements
Stop the browser's default behavior (e.g. form submit page reload, link navigation)
questions.explanation: preventDefault() stops the browser's built-in action. For a form submit, it prevents page reload. For a link click, it prevents navigation. stopPropagation() handles bubbling.

questions.question: What is event delegation?
options: Passing the event to another function
Attaching one listener to a parent element to handle events from its children
Delegating event handling to the server
questions.explanation: Event delegation attaches ONE listener to a parent and uses event.target to determine which child was clicked. It works for dynamically added children and is more memory-efficient than one listener per child.

faq.q: What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
faq.a: event.target is the element that was actually clicked (possibly a child). event.currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to. When using event delegation, these are different — target is the child, currentTarget is the parent.

faq.q: How do I remove an event listener?
faq.a: Use removeEventListener with the exact same function reference: const handler = () => {...}; el.addEventListener('click', handler); el.removeEventListener('click', handler). Arrow functions defined inline cannot be removed. Alternatively, use {once: true} to auto-remove after the first fire.
